title: The data-center land rush
dek: AI compute demand turns land, power, and cooling into the scarce inputs of the decade.
one_sentence: The machines need electricity more than real estate, and whoever controls that grid connection owns the next decade of infrastructure.
lede: For a hundred years, data meant a physical place: a building with machines inside. Now the building doesn't matter. The only thing that matters is whether the grid has enough power to run it. AI training workloads demand 30 to 100+ kilowatts per rack. That flipped the constraint from land to electricity—and from a problem utilities manage slowly to a problem companies must solve fast.
what_changed:
Until 2020, data-center companies competed on square footage. You leased space, filled it with servers, paid the power bill. The colocation industry was worth $13.2 billion in 2021. Today it is $72.37 billion (2026)—a fivefold jump in five years. But that growth is almost entirely about electricity, not space. North American colocation occupancy hit 1% vacancy by 2026. There is nowhere left to build. Operators have stopped trying to acquire land and started fighting for grid connections instead.

The numbers show the severity. US data center electricity demand jumped from 23 gigawatts in 2023 to 42 gigawatts in 2026. Wholesale electricity prices near major data centers climbed 267% in that window. Capacity prices in PJM—the grid operator serving the East Coast and industrial Midwest—jumped 833% in one year alone. These are not incremental changes. This is scarcity.

The real constraint is the queue. American grids are jammed. The interconnection queue—the waiting list for new power connections—exceeds 1,400 gigawatts of stuck requests. A company ordering a new high-capacity connection to the grid now waits four to five years. In saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix, there is no spare capacity at all. Seven major AI companies (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, xAI) signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge with the White House in March 2026 to directly fund grid infrastructure improvements, signaling a historic flip: they no longer wait for utilities to solve power problems. They solve them themselves. The data processing and hosting industry is spending $630 billion on infrastructure in 2026 (up 36% from 2025), with $450 billion explicitly targeted at AI—chips, GPUs, accelerators, and the power systems to run them. Consolidation is accelerating fast. CoreWeave acquired Core Scientific. Equinix closed a $15 billion joint venture with GIC to build hyperscale facilities. Digital Realty acquired Slough (July 2024) and is expanding into new geographies. The colocation market grew 11.5% annually from 2025 to 2026, and will grow another 11.5% through 2030, but only for operators who control power.

Regulation is tightening around the shortage. Oregon signed the POWER Act in August 2025, mandating ten-year power-purchase agreements for facilities over 20 megawatts. California and Virginia implemented large-load tariffs with 25-40 megawatt thresholds. FERC issued data-center-specific transmission tariffs for PJM in December 2025, effective January 2026. These rules acknowledge the new reality: data centers are now essential grid assets. They are no longer just tenants. They are infrastructure.

win: Power companies, transmission operators, and large landowners in high-capacity grid zones (Texas, Oregon, Northern Virginia) win decisively. Electricity becomes the new collateral. A parcel near a substation with spare grid capacity is now worth as much as a pharmaceutical patent. Hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta) and specialized AI hosting platforms (CoreWeave) win because they can absorb $630 billion in capital spending and negotiate directly with utilities and governments. Smaller operators can still win if they specialize in edge compute, liquid cooling, or power-adjacent services—filling the gaps hyperscalers leave behind. Utility companies and grid operators win because they suddenly have leverage. They are no longer afterthoughts. They are dealmakers.
lose: Regional carriers and small-to-mid-sized colocation companies get squeezed. If you don't own a power connection or land near one, you are out. Pricing power for colocation jumped 17-19% in the last two years after 15 years of decline. Occupancy is 1% vacancy nationwide. You cannot grow without electricity access, and electricity access is locked up or years away. Real estate developers who built data centers as speculative plays (betting on rising square-footage demand) lose. The constraint shifted from land to power; vacant facilities in low-capacity grid areas are stranded assets. Workers in areas without data-center buildout lose as well—talent and high-wage jobs concentrate in Texas, Northern Virginia, and other power-rich zones. The rural areas that thought they would get a data center boom get nothing.
worry: The grid itself is not built for this. Interconnection queues exceed 1,400 gigawatts. That is more than the entire US generates on an average day. Utilities move slowly; AI companies move fast. The gap between their timelines is widening. Regulators are tightening rules (Oregon PPAs, FERC tariffs, state large-load regulations) to formalize data centers as infrastructure partners, but those rules can also slow projects or force them into unfavorable terms. The single biggest risk is grid failure—not a blackout, but rolling undersupply where demand overwhelms available generation and transmission in pockets of the country. If a hyperscaler cannot get new grid capacity for two more years, but its training workload is scheduled to double in eighteen months, it either fails to deliver or it pulls power from the rest of the grid, raising costs for everyone else. That is already happening in PJM, where data-center loads are forcing reliability discussions and new tariff rules. One bad grid event—a summer heat spike that triggers cascading line failures while data centers run at peak—could force rationing or brown-outs in major metro areas tied to the same grid. That would turn data-center siting from a competitive advantage into a regulatory and political liability.

title: The Pipes to the Internet
dek: AI's compute sprawl is forcing a reshuffling of who owns the last mile and who hosts the workloads.
one_sentence: Data centers need fiber, bandwidth, and hosting stacks—and the companies that supply them are seeing unprecedented demand, consolidation, and margin squeeze all at once.
lede: The internet's plumbing was designed for browsing and video streaming. Now it's designed for machine learning. That simple shift—from millions of people pulling content to millions of GPUs pushing and pulling petabytes—is remaking the ISP and hosting industries faster than anyone thought possible. Fiber is suddenly critical. So is compute hosting. And everyone is scrambling to supply both.
what_changed:
Internet Service Providers have gone from defending their legacy video bundles to racing for fiber dominance. The US ISP market sits at $179.9 billion in 2026, growing 4.5% year-over-year, but the growth masks a brutal reshuffling underneath. Fiber-to-the-home availability jumped from 37% of US addresses in 2024 to 57% by early 2026—nearly a 20-point sprint in two years. That sprint is federally funded (the BEAD program, now in earnest construction across 46 states with NIST approval in 52 states with grant funds available) and corporate-driven (AT&T targets 60 million locations by 2030; Charter is investing $11.4 billion in capex for 2026 alone). The economics are clear: whoever lays fiber first captures the data center customer. But consolidation is the real story. The number of ISP establishments actually shrunk as the market expanded. Verizon closed a $20 billion Frontier acquisition in March 2026, leapfrogging to second-largest broadband provider. Charter is acquiring Cox Communications by mid-2026. DigitalBridge and Crestview scooped up WideOpenWest for $1.5 billion in 2025. North American ISP M&A hit $81 billion in 2024, doubling the prior year. Smaller ISPs are exiting or being absorbed. The margin squeeze is relentless. ISP profit margins sit around 33.82% (broader information services sector, 2025), but rising capex for fiber buildout and labor costs are eating into that. Meanwhile, legacy revenue streams are collapsing: Comcast lost 322,000 TV subscribers and 65,000 internet subscribers in Q1 2026 alone, forcing ISPs to chase data center customers just to offset the bleeding.

Internet Hosting Services face a different but equally intense squeeze. The market was $98.1 billion in 2025, growing 4.9% year-over-year, but that's a sharp slowdown from the pandemic boom—2020-2022 saw 11.9% growth; now the industry is maturing and fragmenting. Cloud giants (AWS at 31% market share, Azure at 23-25%, Google Cloud at 11-12% in Q1 2026) have encroached on traditional hosting, offering managed infrastructure that undercuts pure hosting providers on price and flexibility. Within the pure hosting sector, consolidation and specialization accelerate. Newfold Digital consolidated Web.com into Network Solutions in June 2025, sunsetting Web.com as a standalone brand. The result: 13,817 hosting establishments as of 2022 are now fighting harder for niches. Price competition is brutal. Labor costs are rising 7% annually for hosting technicians. And compliance is becoming a permanent operational cost—GDPR, CPRA, LGPD are now table-stakes in every contract. The survival strategy is AI automation. In 2025-2026, 65% of hosting providers prioritized AI-powered malware detection, and 53% cited AI-driven automation as critical to 2026 competitiveness. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud all published carbon-aware routing and per-region carbon intensity APIs in Q1 2026, embedding sustainability into hosting decisions. Google cut compute pricing 8% across all regions to fight for share.

The convergence is clear: fiber ISPs and hosting providers are now competing in the same game—capturing data center customers. ISP margins are solid but capex-intensive. Hosting margins are thin (around 5% of revenue in 2022, pressured downward since) but automation-intensive. The winners are the vertically integrated giants—Amazon, Google, Microsoft—who own or control both infrastructure and the pipes. The squeezed are the mid-market ISPs that lag on fiber deployment, and the thousands of small hosting providers that can't afford the AI tooling and compliance burden.

win: Winners own both pipes and computing. Amazon Web Services ($37.59 billion revenue, up 28% year-over-year in Q1 2026), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud control the market consolidation—they own or partner for fiber, sell hosting, and integrate AI tools (Azure with OpenAI GPT-5, AWS with proprietary ML services). Independent hosting providers face a margin trap: rising labor costs (technician wages up 7% annually), price competition from cloud giants cutting by 8%, and compliance burden (GDPR, CPRA, LGPD) that requires permanent engineering headcount. worry: The single biggest risk is stranded infrastructure and regulatory capture. Fiber buildout is racing (46-52 states approved for BEAD), but if demand for data center connectivity outpaces ISP ability to build, prices will spike—attracting new competitors but also inviting antitrust scrutiny. If large ISPs use paid prioritization to favor their own cloud hosting or content partners, smaller hosters and ISPs get locked out, and consolidation accelerates. The regulatory tug-of-war (five states—CA, WA, OR, CO, VT—maintained local net neutrality protections) could create fragmentation that raises costs for everyone.

title: The software that runs on top
dek: Where enterprise software vendors are fighting for survival as AI reshapes what their products are worth.
lede: The data centers eating terawatts need software to run them. That software layer is in crisis. Not because it's broken—because AI is making it obsolete faster than vendors can pivot. Every SaaS company is now scrambling to prove AI makes them essential instead of replaceable.
what_changed:
AI has turned enterprise software into a cannibal game. Customer relationship management, business intelligence, workflow automation, customer support—entire product categories are getting gutted by AI agents that do the work these tools were designed for. In February 2026, $2 trillion in software sector market cap evaporated in what traders called the "SaaSpocalypse" as fear of disruption peaked. But that wasn't the bottom. By March 2026, Deutsche Bank declared "peak fear," signaling the bottom was in. The market bifurcated. Salesforce, recognizing the threat, went on an acquisition spree: Informatica in November 2025 for data integration and AI pipelines, Qualified.com in April 2026 for AI-driven sales, and Fin in June 2026—a pure AI customer support and sales agent. Total M&A activity for the year hit $440 billion, with 72% of SaaS acquisition targets in 2025 pitching AI as their sole value proposition. Acquiring companies no longer care about feature breadth; they're buying AI-first capabilities or not buying at all.

The database and storage layer shows the same pattern on steroids. Databricks reached $5.4 billion in ARR with 65% growth in February 2026, while Snowflake, the most-used data warehouse vendor, grew at 29% year-over-year to $4.68 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue. But here's the squeeze: Databricks is worth 2x Snowflake's valuation despite similar revenue. The market is paying for AI-native data platforms, not traditional warehouses. Every major cloud provider is embedding vector search and AI optimization directly into their databases. AWS upgraded Aurora Serverless on April 20, 2026, promising 30% faster scaling for AI workloads with vector search as standard. Microsoft added vector indexes to Azure SQL Hyperscale on March 18, 2026. Google AlloyDB gained auto-embedding functions on January 2, 2026. This is a systematic dismantling of the licensing model. Traditional databases—Oracle, SQL Server—face sustained pricing pressure as customers standardize on managed cloud services. Perpetual enterprise licensing is dead; consumption-based subscriptions with outcome-based pricing are taking over. By 2025, 61% of companies had already shifted to hybrid pricing with base fees plus usage metering. Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise SaaS will be outcome-based by 2026.

Complexity is the third killer. The average enterprise now manages 354 APIs, up from 200 two years earlier. Every time a company adds a new system—and AI is forcing them to add new systems constantly—the integration nightmare grows. SMB and mid-market vendors are getting trapped between cloud giants who can afford to be free or $1/month and specialized players who are moving upmarket into AI analytics, real-time processing, and agentic automation. The small vendor is dead. Regulatory complexity compounds the squeeze. GDPR fines exceeded $6.2 billion through August 2025. DORA enforcement went live in 2026 with mandatory database-layer change management requirements. These aren't one-time costs; they're structural. Every database vendor now has to build compliance infrastructure into the product, raising the engineering bar and making customer acquisition more expensive.

The enterprise software market crossed $317.5 billion in 2026 with a 13.8% year-over-year growth rate, and it's supposed to add 38,732 new workers to reach 179,869 employees by 2026 from 141,137 in 2021. But those growth numbers mask the carnage underneath: margin compression, consolidation, pricing model whiplash, and the existential dread that your product—no matter how much your engineers love it—could be replaced by an AI agent trained on a few hundred examples. Vendors are no longer selling software. They're selling data pipelines, AI model training infrastructure, and the promise that they'll survive long enough to stay compliant.

win: Specialized, AI-native vendors in databases (Databricks, Snowflake), data integration (post-Informatica Salesforce), and cloud infrastructure (AWS, Microsoft, Google) capture the value. They own the layer that trains AI models and the infrastructure AI needs to run. Legacy perpetual licensing vendors get squeezed; acquisition targets get absorbed into larger platforms. Cloud giants win because they can bundle AI into databases for free, commoditizing competitors' core products. Vendors selling AI-first solutions—agent platforms, real-time analytics, agentic automation—command valuation premiums because they're perceived as solving the next problem, not the last one.
lose: Mid-market and SMB software vendors are trapped. Too small to compete with cloud giants; too general-purpose to avoid cannibalization by AI agents. Traditional database licensing vendors (Oracle, SQL Server) face sustained pricing pressure as customers shift to managed cloud services. Customer support software, CRM features, workflow automation tools—any software that automates routine knowledge work—is now a liability on a company's product portfolio because customers know AI can do it better. Employees at traditional software companies watch market cap evaporate and acquisition multiples collapse while they're told to "add AI" to products that are fundamentally being made redundant.
worry: The cascade: If AI can automate the software engineer's job tomorrow—writing code, debugging, shipping features—then every software company is a potential target for the same force squeezing their customers. A software engineer's productivity spike from AI tooling (Copilot, Claude, etc.) compresses the time to feature parity, which collapses the moat that once justified licensing fees. The worry is that the entire industry hits deflation in 2027 or 2028 as companies realize their software stack is 80% commodity + 20% differentiation, and 70% of that differentiation can now be built by a team of five instead of fifty. That's not disruption; that's structural contraction.
one_sentence: AI is cannibalizing enterprise software's value while forcing vendors to chase cloud giants into infrastructure and agents, leaving anyone selling traditional tools or mid-market SMB solutions in existential peril.

title: The Generation Scramble
dek: Data centers need firm power now—gas utilities are racing to expand, solar is splitting in two, and the grid is at a breaking point.
lede: AI's power hunger flipped the electricity market overnight. Utilities that spent a decade preparing for coal to die and renewables to rise are now frantically building new natural gas plants. The grid's transmission is so clogged that solar farms can't connect for years. And residential solar, which relied on a federal tax credit for two decades, just got it cut off. Everything plugged into electricity is about to get more expensive and harder to find.
what_changed:
Natural gas just became the infrastructure play of the decade. In March 2026, NextEra Energy announced a historic 10 GW expansion of natural gas capacity in Texas and Pennsylvania—approved by the Trump administration and directly tied to AI data center demand. This wasn't a gradual forecast; it catalyzed a industry-wide pivot. Duke Energy committed $103 billion in capital spending (2026-2030) and is seeking 10 GW of new gas procurement in the Carolinas. Southern Company followed suit. The natural gas market is now $105.2 billion in the US (2026) with margins widening; utilities are treating data center customers as the new industrial anchor tenant. This is a genuine reversal. Natural gas had been declining as a share of electricity generation as renewables rose, but in 2026 it sits at 40% of generation, down from 42% in 2024 only because Henry Hub prices surged 60% in 2025 and are forecast to rise another 30% by 2027. Coal is now cheaper in the margin, so utilities are burning more of it—coal climbed to 17% of generation in 2025 before settling back to 15% in 2026—but coal plants are aging and retiring, so they can't scale. Natural gas is the only fuel that can ramp fast and meet long-term contracts. The paradox: data centers want zero-carbon power, but they're forcing a gas buildout because the grid can't connect renewables fast enough.

Solar shows what happens when you split an industry in two. Utility-scale solar is in a construction frenzy. Developers safe-harbored 216-240 GW of capacity ahead of the July 4, 2026 federal deadline under the Inflation Reduction Act and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Texas alone will host 40% of new 2026 capacity. But here's the trap: the interconnection queue is jammed. The US grid now has 2,600 GW of projects waiting to connect, with a median wait time of five years. Solar farms take 1-5 years to build. Transmission takes 10-15 years. So massive solar capacity is being built and stuck offline, unable to feed the grid. Meanwhile, the PPA (Power Purchase Agreement) price for solar hit $64.49/MWh in Q1 2026, up sharply from the $40s range in prior years because tariffs (polysilicon tariffs doubled in January 2025) and shipping costs spiked. The residential half is collapsing. The 30% federal tax credit expired on December 31, 2025, after 20 years of dominating the financing model. Roughly 100 solar companies have gone bankrupt since 2023; Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025, and Sunrun entered distress. Financing froze—banks stopped investing in tax-credit instruments. Third-party ownership (TPO) models now capture 65% of residential deals, but even that can't offset the credit loss. Residential solar went from the driver of the industry to a clearance bin.

Wind is caught between boom and squeeze. Onshore wind added a remarkable 8.2 GW in 2025, a sharp reversal after a 2024 lull. Data centers are driving this—wind is now the cheapest way to meet long-term power contracts, so developers are racing to build. But tariffs and permitting are shredding margins. Steel tariffs went from 25% in March 2025 to 50% in June 2025, raising turbine component costs by 25-30% for imported parts. EBIT margins compressed from 21.5% in 2022 to 15-17% in 2026. GE Vernova invested $600 million in US factory capacity as a tariff hedge, signaling that manufacturing onshore is now cheaper than importing. The industry split between onshore (81.9% of revenue) and offshore (18%) is widening. Onshore is riding demand, but offshore entered crisis: Ørsted canceled projects, citing supply-chain inflation, rising interest rates, and construction risk. A December 2025 court victory temporarily blocked an executive order freezing federal wind development, but policy volatility remains the operational risk.

Hydroelectric power is the wild card nobody planned for. The western drought is relentless. Lake Powell could hit minimum power pool by December 2026, potentially halting generation at the worst moment. The Colorado River Basin is 100% in drought as of 2025, having lost 27.8 million acre-feet of groundwater since 2002. Hydropower generation reached 245 billion kWh in 2025, a recovery from 2024's record low, but the EIA projects only 259 billion kWh in 2026—that's 1.8% below the 10-year average. Snow drought—record warmth causing early snowmelt—has replaced traditional drought as the operational enemy. Yet private capital is flooding in. Hydropower companies raised $718 million in equity in 2025 (up from $167 million in 2024), and the DOE identified nearly 97,000 non-powered dams suitable for retrofitting. Government funding hit a record: $430 million in incentive payments to 293 projects plus $220 million annual congressional appropriation. The bet is on small hydro and distributed generation to replace what western drought is taking away. But that's years out, and the grid needs power now.

Natural gas plants are the only infrastructure that can ramp fast enough to meet multi-year power contracts with AI companies. Margin expansion and government backing (Trump administration approved NextEra's 10 GW expansion in March 2026) make this a once-in-a-decade capital story. Onshore wind developers win the second-place prize because data centers are locking in long-term PPAs, making wind cheaper than other options—but only if tariffs stabilize. Private hydroelectric companies are beginning to win on smaller scales as the DOE and Congress fund distributed generation ($430 million in 2026 alone) and retrofitted dams offer lower risk than massive greenfield plants.
lose: Residential solar companies lost everything when the tax credit expired December 31, 2025. Over a hundred went bankrupt; Sunnova, Sunrun, and mid-market installers are in distress. Homeowners who needed the 30% credit to afford solar are priced out. Transmission developers and grid planners are squeezed because they have to connect 2,600 GW of projects with five-year wait times while solar and wind farms sit offline. Coal-dependent utilities are caught: coal's cheaper in the margin right now, but coal plants are aging, retirement orders are sticky, and they can't build new ones. The western US loses out if Lake Powell hits minimum power pool by December 2026—cities, agriculture, and existing hydro generation all face curtailment. Offshore wind is nearly dead, with Ørsted canceling projects and no recovery in sight.
worry: The biggest risk is a cascade failure in the western grid. Lake Powell could hit minimum power pool by December 2026. If that happens, hydropower generation halts at the exact moment data centers are demanding maximum power. The grid's interconnection queue (2,600 GW, five-year median wait) means utilities can't respond fast. They'll turn to whatever power is dispatchable—natural gas. That drives gas prices higher, squeezes margins across electricity, and forces rolling demand destruction across all of customer. Meanwhile, solar capacity is being built but can't connect, so it's stranded offline. Transmission infrastructure takes 10-15 years to build, but solar farms and wind turbines take 1-5 years. This mismatch will persist through the 2030s, making blackout risk the shadow cost of the data-center boom.

title: The grid bottleneck
dek: Transmission and gas delivery, not generation, are the real constraint—and whoever controls the pipes to data centers wins.
lede: The US power grid is hitting a hard wall. Data centers alone will consume 75.8 gigawatts by 2026, and renewables keep adding unpredictability on top of that. The problem is not that we can't generate electricity anymore—it's that we can't move it fast enough. Transmission got stuck in a permitting nightmare while everyone built generators.
what_changed:
The grid used to be a simple model: utilities built wires, people paid rates, the margin stayed steady at 7–8% forever. That's over. Data center demand outran transmission capacity in 2025, forcing utilities to book record profit margins—up to 15% of revenue in some regions like Florida Power & Light (27.4% in 2025-2026) and Mid-American Energy (27.6%)—double the historical norm. The real bottleneck is not generation or money; it's the interconnection queue. FERC's transmission system has become so toxic that tech giants and power companies stopped trusting it. Instead, hyperscalers announced 101 gigawatts of behind-the-meter natural gas generation to bypass the grid entirely—a structural revolt against waiting years for permitting. In PJM, the wholesale power market, capacity costs spiked 262% in 2025, and spot power prices jumped 49%, because data center demand ran headfirst into a transmission grid designed for slower growth. The math is brutal: data centers will gobble 90 gigawatts of peak load growth by 2026, but existing wires can't deliver it fast enough.

Natural gas is now pinched from two sides. Industrial consumption hit a record 23.6 billion cubic feet per day in 2025, driven by both manufacturing and those same data centers running backup generators 24/7. Retail gas prices rose 60% in 2025 versus 2024, but regulated utilities can't pass that on fast enough—their margins got squeezed even as input costs spiked. Henry Hub, the benchmark, is forecast at $3.67 per million BTU for 2026, elevated and volatile. Meanwhile, LNG exports are booming: US capacity will grow from 11.4 Bcf/d in early 2024 to 28.7 Bcf/d by 2029. That export push locked in high prices and prioritized foreign buyers over domestic grid stability. Behind all this, pipeline operators added 12.8 Bcf/d of new gas transmission in 2024–2025 and have another 44.9 Bcf/d queued for 2026–2027, mostly from the Permian. The paradox: pipelines get built on cost-plus FERC regulation, so revenue is tied to what regulators allow, not price movements. Kinder Morgan, the largest, posted record 2025 earnings of $16.9 billion, up 12%, because the system rewards scale and throughput, not efficiency.

Transmission and distribution, the actual wires that move power to your door, are now the commanding position. The market grew to $536.2 billion in 2025, up from $476.1 billion in 2022, and utilities are racing to raise capital. The grid investment plan is $1.4 trillion for 2025–2030, but permitting delays mean each year lost is money lost and data center projects get cancelled or shifted to willing jurisdictions. FERC Order No. 1920 in late 2025 tried to fix this with new transmission planning reforms, and a new ruling on large load interconnection is due April 30, 2026, but compliance will take years. The bigger shift: consolidation. NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy announced a $66.8 billion merger, the largest utility deal in 2025, to secure generation and transmission assets ahead of the grid crunch. Utilities now have pricing power they never had before. Margins climbed because demand is inelastic—data centers can't just move elsewhere, and people still need power—while supply is constrained. The transmission grid became the narrow gate everyone must pass through, and whoever owns it can charge what the market will bear.

Battery storage, the wild card, exploded from 15 gigawatts added in 2025 to 24 gigawatts planned for 2026. This isn't solving the grid problem; it's reshaping how transmission operators manage it. Batteries let them absorb renewable intermittency without building new wires, but only if they have enough capacity nearby. This incentivizes data centers to co-locate batteries and gas generators with servers, further fragmenting the grid into hyperscaler-owned microgrids. The natural outcome: the utilities that survive are the ones that upgrade their transmission fast enough to handle local demand spikes, lock in long-term data center contracts, and control the gas pipelines that feed backup generators. Everyone else—mid-size distributors, independent power producers like Pine Gate Renewables (which filed bankruptcy in November 2025)—gets squeezed out of the value chain.

lose: Mid-size utilities and independent power producers get squeezed. Residential and commercial customers lose too—utilities are raising rates aggressively to cover transmission buildout, and those rate hikes flow through to everyone on the grid, not just data centers.
worry: The biggest risk is that the grid fractures. Utilities need that load to justify $1.4 trillion in transmission spending, but if data centers exit the public grid entirely, the utility business model breaks—regulated retail rates can't cover the sunk cost of wires nobody uses anymore. Meanwhile, FERC's April 30, 2026 deadline for large load interconnection rules might come too late: by then, every tech giant with a data center will have already built their own gas generator to avoid the wait. The grid becomes a managed decline for midsize cities and rural areas, while data centers cluster in hyperscaler-friendly zones with dedicated transmission and cheap gas. That's not a grid anymore; it's two parallel networks, one working and one left behind.

title: The Electrical Trades Cash In
dek: Electricians, HVAC techs, and turbine makers are the picks-and-shovels of the compute buildout, and they're getting rich while labor scarce and tariffs squeeze competitors.
lede: The compute super-cycle has turned the electrical and mechanical trades from boring infrastructure work into the bottleneck that limits how fast AI can be built. Electricians are in acute shortage. HVAC contractors are commanding premium rates. Turbine and engine makers face regulatory deadlines they can't dodge and tariff costs they can't escape. This is not a nice problem to have if you're in one of these trades—it's a license to print money, at least for now.
what_changed:
Electricians, historically caught between a dying residential market and flat commercial demand, have suddenly become the scarce labor holding back data-center construction. In 2026, data-center electrical work alone reached $50.7 billion annually, up 28 percent year-over-year. That surge is real and growing faster than the industry can supply labor. The US electricians market is $370.9 billion in 2026, but growth is modest overall—down 1.1 percent in 2026—because the work is concentrating in high-skill, high-margin specialties (solar, EV charging infrastructure, data-center power distribution) where experienced workers command $76,000 to $110,000+ per year. Tariffs have crushed margins for smaller contractors: copper wiring jumped 18 percent in price, electrical panels up 22 percent, because the tariff wave on imported materials hit steel, aluminum, and components at 25 percent rates starting in 2024. Smaller contractors with thin 5-6 percent margins can't absorb those shocks. The result is consolidation: private equity platforms are aggressively rolling up fragmented electrical firms, even as deal count dropped to 99 in 2025 from 140 in 2024, because those that survive need scale to negotiate tariff-driven material costs and capture the high-margin data-center and infrastructure work.

HVAC contractors face a different squeeze—a clean bifurcation between a dying residential market and an exploding commercial one. Residential HVAC work, which was 46 percent of the industry's 2022 revenue, is collapsing because mortgage rates stuck near 6 percent killed new home construction; single-family starts fell 5 percent in 2025 to 909,000 units. But commercial HVAC is booming. Data centers, office buildings, and warehouses are on modernization binges driven by energy-efficiency mandates, indoor air quality rules, and AI-powered building automation. The market is $159.4 billion in 2026, growing just 2.6 percent overall, but commercial HVAC is expanding at 8.27 percent annually. On top of that, the EPA phased out R-410A refrigerant on January 1, 2025, and the sell-through deadline hit on January 1, 2026—every new residential unit now requires A2L refrigerants (R-454B, R-32). That forced technicians to retrain, systems to be redesigned, and installation costs to jump 10 percent. Heat pumps have hit an inflection point: they outsold central air conditioners and gas furnaces for the first time in 2025, and over 48 percent of US homes now use electrical heating. This is good for commercial contractors and bad for traditional residential shops. Labor is brutal: the industry has 590,000 employees with acute shortages pushing wages up 8 percent annually. Private equity has noticed—PE add-on acquisitions in HVAC jumped 88 percent year-over-year through mid-2025, with platforms like Apex Service Partners (Apollo-backed, ~$10 billion) rolling up over 100 brands and closing 60 add-ons in 2025 alone.

Turbine and engine makers operate under a different kind of pressure. The US engine and turbine manufacturing industry is $55.0 billion in 2026, growing only 1.6 percent, but the real story is tariffs and regulatory deadlines. Tariffs on imported steel, aluminum, and engine components are running at 25 percent, and that alone cost major producers like Caterpillar an estimated $2.2 to $2.4 billion in 2026. Some firms are reshoring components and locking in long-term US supplier contracts, raising operating leverage but spreading execution risk across the supply chain. The EPA's 2027 heavy-duty engine rule is the hard deadline: NOx limits cut 82 to 90 percent across all new truck, locomotive, and marine engines. Detroit Diesel and Cummins are already shipping Gen-6 and 2027-compliant models, but the technology lift is steep. Truck prices are climbing. Warranty obligations extend 5 to 7 years. The long-haul diesel franchise is secure because electrification is still a fringe play, but the margin pressure is real. GE Vernova is pivoting hard to meet the grid's hunger for new generation capacity: turbine production capacity is moving from 55 to 70-80 heavy-duty turbines annually, with an 80-gigawatt backlog sold out through 2028-2030 and $300 million in capex for South Carolina and New York plants. Cummins launched a 13-liter, 2600 Series multi-fuel engine in 2026 available in diesel, biofuel, and hydrogen at 400 to 700 hp. These firms cannot duck regulation or tariffs. They have to absorb costs, retool fast, and lock in supply chains. The ones with domestic scale and capital to invest are winning. The ones betting on cheap imports are getting crushed.

PE platforms are aggressively rolling up fragmented firms to create scale and capture the consolidation premium.

Single-family housing starts fell 5% to 909,000 units in 2025, collapsing traditional residential HVAC and electrical work. Tariffs hit copper wiring 18% and electrical panels 22%, and small contractors cannot absorb those shocks or negotiate volume discounts. HVAC shops dependent on residential retrofit and new-build work are being squeezed out as commercial work bifurcates and PE platforms consolidate at scale. Engine and turbine makers without domestic supply chains and capital for rapid 2027 EPA compliance retooling face margin compression, warranty cost overruns, and competitive loss to better-capitalized rivals. Import-dependent manufacturers are getting crushed by 25% tariffs on steel, aluminum, and components.
worry: The real bottleneck is labor, not money. Electricians and HVAC technicians are acutely scarce—Nvidia and Microsoft CEOs have publicly cited electrician shortages as a constraint on AI infrastructure expansion. Training pipelines are not growing fast enough to fill the gap, and wages are being bid up 8-9% annually. If the data-center buildout continues at its current $50.7 billion annualized rate, but electrician supply stays flat or shrinks, projects will slip. The 2027 EPA emissions deadline is a hard cliff: firms that miss retooling will be shut out of the truck and engine market entirely. Consolidation is accelerating, which means fewer independent shops and more leverage in the hands of PE platforms—that could squeeze margins downstream and reduce competitive pricing pressure, ultimately making the buildout more expensive.

title: Concrete, Steel & the Shell
dek: AI data centers are eating a generation's worth of cement, steel, and construction labor in five years—whoever can pour concrete fast enough and source carbon steel at scale wins.
lede: Data centers are not just consuming electricity. They are physical machines made of concrete, steel beams, rebar, and cooling systems—and the sheer velocity of build is making these materials suddenly scarce and expensive. The compute super-cycle is colliding head-on with a construction industry that was already limping: not enough workers, tariff-driven cost spikes, and financing rates that kill traditional projects. This is a story about who gets squeezed out and who gets rich from the buildout.
what_changed:
In 2024, data center construction starts were running at about $400 million per month. By December 2025, they hit $6.5 billion—a 190% surge year-over-year to $77.7 billion annually. The Stargate Project alone ($500 billion over four years, announced January 2025) locked in a decade-plus pipeline. Amazon's $23 billion Ohio expansion and Microsoft's Wisconsin mega-facility are both due live in 2026. This is not gradual. This is a compression of a decade's normal build into five years.

The construction industry's capacity did not double. The US cement industry operates at 102-105 million metric tons annually—that ceiling has been flat for five years. Consumption sits at 105-108 million tons. The gap is covered by 25-26 million tons of imports, roughly 21% of apparent consumption in 2025. When a 25% tariff on cement took effect in April 2025, Canadian and Mexican imports became uncompetitive overnight. Domestic production cannot expand—there are only five major firms (LafargeHolcim, Martin Marietta, CEMEX, HeidelbergCement, Buzzi Unicem), and new kiln capacity takes three to five years to build. The data center buildout is now competing for the same concrete tonnage that keeps roads, bridges, and warehouses going. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) deployed only $500 billion of its $1.2 trillion commitment by September 2025—but that created a multi-year pipeline of 207,000+ miles of roadway and 11,400+ bridge projects underway. Both demand cement. At the same time.

The labor shortage is worse than the material shortage. Commercial building construction employed 249,166 workers in 2022. It needs 277,367 by 2027. That's a 500,000-worker gap across the whole industry—the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates it costs the sector $10.8 billion annually. Crane operators, concrete finishers, ironworkers, and heavy-equipment operators are not sitting idle. They are pricing their time aggressively. Wage inflation in construction outpaced general inflation by 3-4 percentage points in 2025. The firms that can move fastest—the mega-contractors consolidating through M&A (562 deals in 2025, up 18.2% from 2024)—are snapping up crews and entire firms. Mid-market contractors are losing bids because they cannot staff the crew. Data center builders have deep pockets and urgency. They win the bidding war. Office construction, retail renovation, and mid-market warehouse builds all get pushed down the queue or cancelled.

By 2026, the commercial building construction market will be split in two. Data centers are the only engine: the $77.7 billion in 2025 starts seeded by Stargate, Amazon, and Microsoft will sustain $315.5 billion in total commercial construction, but concentrated in power, cooling, and land prep. Traditional office construction is at a 10-year low—office demand fell 41% since 2019, new deliveries dropped 26% in 2025, and vacancies are concentrated in older Class-B and Class-C buildings. Retail and hospitality are soft but stable. The tariff on cement (now 25% for most sources, 46% for Vietnam) has shrunk import competition and raised prices. Portland-limestone cement (PLC, Type IL) dominates the market—all 50 states approved it by April 2024, and 97% of blended cement shipments are now PLC. This shift happened because PLC cuts CO2 by 10% and fits into federal infrastructure mandates, but it also requires capital investment and retooling. The firms investing now (like CRH, which acquired Eco Material Technologies in July 2025, and Martin Marietta, which swapped assets with QuikCrete in Q1 2026) are positioning for long-term margin. The firms that do not invest are losing share to tariff-trapped competitors.

A single delayed mega-facility cascades: cloud providers miss AI training deadlines, chip makers backpedal, and the entire economic thesis of "compute is the new commodity" stalls. title: When Power Gets Scarce
dek: AI data centers are hoarding the grid—and everyone else is learning to wait for electricity.

They need reliable power to run 24/7, but data centers get priority in the interconnection queue and better rates through long-term contracts. Independent power producers like Pine Gate get squeezed out entirely—they can't compete for grid access or financing when utilities are locking in generation and transmission assets. States and counties lose planning control. FERC's emergency rulemaking in October 2025 to fast-track data center interconnection overrides local transmission planning. Renewables lose momentum. Utilities are re-gassing with natural gas and coal to keep the lights on for data centers, not building transmission fast enough to absorb wind and solar cheaply. Coal plant retirements hit a 15-year low—only 2.6 GW retired in 2025 versus 8.5 GW planned—because utilities are now keeping them running as backup capacity.
worry: The single biggest risk is that the grid cannot be built fast enough. Utilities need $1.4 trillion in transmission investment from 2025 to 2030. FERC can issue directives, but construction, permitting, and land rights take years. Meanwhile, data center capacity is being installed in months. If the transmission queue stays toxic—if projects still face approval delays and grid constraints—some data centers will never turn on, or they'll move to regions where power is cheaper (overseas, mostly). That kills the whole buildout story. The other risk: utilities are locking in natural gas and coal contracts that last decades, betting on their coal fleets running till 2045 or later. If renewables actually do scale up faster than expected—battery costs drop 40% in five years, solar installs surge—those utilities are stranded with expensive, aging fossil fuel plants that can't compete. They'll try to shift costs to ratepayers. Regulations will follow. The third risk is regional instability. A few utilities controlling generation, transmission, and data center contracts in Texas or the Carolinas creates chokepoint pricing. If NextEra or Duke Energy faces a cyberattack, a physical outage, or regulatory pressure, the whole region's data center economy goes dark. No redundancy. Centralizing power infrastructure to serve centralized AI compute is the opposite of resilient.
one_sentence: Data centers are eating the grid, and anyone who can't pay premium rates or build their own power plant is getting left behind.

title: Heat, water & the environment
dek: AI's cooling needs are making water scarce and turning waste into assets — while exposing the limits of an aging hydroelectric grid.
one_sentence: Data centers are draining rivers and heating aquifers, but turning waste heat into renewable power and forcing utilities to rethink infrastructure for a hotter, thirstier future.
lede: The compute super-cycle didn't just create demand for electricity — it created an entirely new constraint: water and the heat that comes with it. Cooling a data center the size of a small town takes as much water as a mid-size city. That water has to come from somewhere. Rivers are drying out. Aquifers are dropping. And the waste heat pouring out of servers is too much to ignore anymore — nobody can just dump millions of tons of thermal energy into the air or water and pretend it's fine.
what_changed:
The waste-to-energy plant business — the US industry that burns garbage to make electricity — is caught at an inflection point. The sector pulled in $1.4 billion in 2025 and operates 64 plants across 21 states. These plants used to be about incineration and getting rid of waste. Now they're suddenly interesting to data center operators hunting for reliable baseload power to run AI clusters. Data center electricity consumption surged 17% in 2025. AI-focused data centers are tripling their power use. Tech companies signed 40% of all corporate renewable energy power-purchase agreements in 2025. That demand is real. But the WTE industry faces its own squeeze: landfill gas capture is eating its lunch. There are now 598 landfill gas systems in the US producing 64% of renewable natural gas as of 2025. Twenty new landfill gas projects launched in 2025 alone, adding 39.9 billion cubic feet of biogas capacity. An updated EPA methane rule that takes effect in 2027 is expected to push 705 additional landfills into capture projects. Reworld — the company that owns most of the major plants after buying Covanta in 2024 — processes 20.8 million tons of waste annually and is retargeting itself toward materials recovery, not just burning. The economics tell the story: WTE plants are pulling 18-25% EBITDA margins in 2025, down from 25-30% at landfill gas operators. That gap is where the pain is.

Hydroelectric power is in crisis, and it's a crisis that hits data centers directly. The US hydroelectric sector generated 245 billion kWh in 2025, but the EIA projects only 259 billion kWh in 2026 — that's still 1.8% below the 10-year average. The problem is simple: the West is drying out. Lake Powell, the Colorado River's second-largest reservoir, could hit minimum power pool by December 2026, potentially halting generation at the worst time. The Colorado River Basin is 100% in drought as of 2025 and has lost 27.8 million acre-feet of groundwater since 2002. Snow drought — unseasonably warm years causing early snowmelt — has replaced traditional drought as the real threat to generation. This isn't a cyclical downturn. This is structural. The sector is fighting back with capital. Private equity raised $718 million in equity for hydropower in 2025, up 433% from $167 million in 2024. The DOE announced $430 million in incentive payments to 293 projects at 212 facilities in 2026, and Congress appropriated $220 million annual funding for hydropower and marine research — the highest on record. The agency identified nearly 97,000 non-powered dams suitable for retrofitting. But retrofitting takes years. Licensing bottlenecks are still there. And the core problem — drought and climate volatility — can't be willed away with capital alone.

The waste heat coming out of data centers is starting to look like an asset. A single large AI data center can dump the thermal energy equivalent of a small power plant into the atmosphere or local water body. That heat, if captured and used, could heat homes, greenhouses, or industrial processes. Some operators are already experimenting with pipe-to-district-heating schemes, particularly in cold climates. The Reworld rebranding signals that the waste-to-energy industry is pivoting: instead of pure incineration, they're targeting materials recovery, alternative fuels, and now waste heat capture. Enerkem's Ecoplanta project in Spain received approval in January 2025 for waste-to-methanol conversion, signaling an industry-wide shift toward advanced chemical recycling and using waste as feedstock, not just fuel for burning. These shifts matter because they reframe waste from a liability into an input. Data centers are creating new markets for waste heat and biogas as baseload power. The constraint was always the grid's ability to absorb that power and the water needed to move the heat around. Now water scarcity is making the whole calculus more expensive and forcing operators to cluster data centers near the few reliable water sources — rivers with good flow, coastal areas, or regions with cheap recycled water.

Traditional landfill operators face a future where new methane rules force them into capture projects they may not want or can afford. title: The Compute Super-Cycle
dek: AI's hunger for power is reshaping the grid and everything plugged into it—whoever has electricity, land, and cooling near the data centers wins a once-in-a-generation buildout.
lede: For 15 years, electricity was cheap and transmission was abundant. That era ended in 2024. AI data centers—training rigs burning 30–100+ kilowatts per rack, inference farms running 10–20 kW steady—have turned the US power grid from a taken-for-granted utility into a scarce, rationed resource. The entire economy is suddenly competing for electrons, and the winners are those who own generation, land, and cooling near demand.
what_changed:
Until 2020, colocation facilities competed on real estate—who had the most square footage. Today they compete on power. The US colocation market reached $72.37 billion in 2026 (up from $46.84 billion in 2025, a 54.6% jump in one year) and occupancy is at 1% vacancy, meaning there is nowhere left to build. The colocation industry's 11.5% CAGR through 2030 masks the real story: pricing has jumped 17–19% in just two years after 15 years of decline. Electricity access, not real estate, is now the moat. The grid cannot keep up. Interconnection queues exceed 1,400 gigawatts of stuck requests, with lead times stretching to four to five years in saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix. Federal regulators (FERC, December 2025) issued data-center-specific transmission tariffs for PJM, and states are rushing their own—Oregon signed the POWER Act in August 2025 mandating 10-year power-purchase agreements for any facility over 20 megawatts.

This squeeze on electricity has catalyzed what utilities are calling "The Great Re-Gassing." Natural gas generation remains at 40% of US electricity in 2026, but in March 2026, NextEra Energy announced a historic 10-gigawatt natural gas expansion in Texas and Pennsylvania, backed by the Trump administration, explicitly to meet AI data center demand. Duke Energy committed $103 billion in capex for 2026–2030, including 10 gigawatts of new gas procurement in the Carolinas. Southern Company is expanding similarly. The coal industry, which had been in steady decline, saw a temporary rebound to 17% generation share in 2025 (from under 15% previously) as Henry Hub natural gas prices surged 60% in 2025 and are forecast to rise another 30% by 2027. Coal retirements hit a 15-year low of 2.6 gigawatts in 2025, delayed by DOE emergency orders to keep plants online. None of this solves the underlying problem: utilities are racing to build generation and transmission infrastructure that will take years to permit and construct, while data centers are arriving now.

The transmission system is the true bottleneck. The electric power transmission market reached $536.2 billion in 2025 (up from $476.1 billion in 2022, a 12.6% increase in three years), but $1.4 trillion in transmission investment is planned for 2025–2030—and that may not be enough. Data centers will consume 75.8 gigawatts by 2026, accounting for nearly 90 gigawatts of total peak load growth. Wholesale power costs in PJM spiked 49% in 2025, with capacity costs up 262%, driven by data center demand outrunning supply. Profit margins at utilities have climbed to 15% of revenue in 2025, double the historical 7–8% norm. Companies like NextEra and Dominion merged in May–June 2026 (a $66.8 billion deal) to secure generation and transmission assets before constraints tighten further. Battery storage deployment is exploding—24 gigawatts planned for 2026 versus 15 gigawatts added in 2025—as operators scramble to buffer intermittent renewables and smooth demand peaks. Tech giants (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta) are responding by investing directly in generation: buying renewable energy, negotiating long-term PPAs, and signing deals with utilities for dedicated capacity.

This buildout is creating a secondary labor shortage. Data center construction spending hit $50.7 billion annualized in April 2026, up 28% year-over-year, and electricians are the constrained input. Journeymen electricians now earn $76,000–$110,000+, with specialists in solar, EV charging, and data center work commanding premium rates. However, tariffs have hit the industry hard: copper wiring prices jumped 18%, electrical panels 22%, squeezing smaller contractors' margins while consolidation accelerates. The electricians industry as a whole is $370.9 billion (2026) and has added businesses at a 3.7% CAGR, but residential construction has collapsed due to high interest rates, forcing the industry to depend on data center work as its growth engine. The structural mismatch is clear: the grid, generation capacity, transmission, and skilled labor are all becoming scarce at the same moment. Whoever owns renewable generation near cooling water, has transmission capacity, controls real estate, or can command electrician labor wins. Everyone else is stuck in a queue.

win: Tech giants (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta) and utilities with existing generation assets or access to renewable energy sources win decisively. They can negotiate long-term PPAs, build their own solar and wind farms near data centers, and secure transmission capacity before constraints tighten. Equinix and Digital Realty, the two largest colocation operators (combined ~20% US share), win by raising prices and controlling capacity-constrained facilities. Renewable energy companies win in the near term by securing long-term power contracts. Utilities with coal or gas plants and transmission assets also win—profit margins have doubled—though the long-term bet is on gas expansion (not coal). Large, well-capitalized electrical contractors with data center specialization win; smaller, undercapitalized firms squeeze out.
lose: Smaller colocation operators who lack power PPAs or renewable generation contracts lose. Residential construction and small electrical contractors lose because talent and capital flow to higher-margin data center work. Consumers face rising electricity rates as utilities pass through interconnection and capital costs. States without natural gas infrastructure or renewable capacity lose—California and the Mid-Atlantic remain capacity-constrained and cannot attract new major facilities. Coal plant workers lose as retirements resume once gas capacity comes online. Independent power producers without long-term contracts (like Pine Gate Renewables, which filed Chapter 11 in November 2025) lose to scale and consolidation.
worry: The single biggest risk is a misalignment between the speed at which data centers are being built and the speed at which the grid can be upgraded. Data center construction is running 28% year-over-year growth, but FERC interconnection rule changes won't take effect until 2026 at the earliest, and transmission buildout takes 5–7 years. If data centers are installed faster than generation and transmission can support them, the grid will experience rolling blackouts, forced demand destruction (shutdowns of data centers or other large loads), and a demand shock that crashes semiconductor and AI chip prices. Alternatively, utilities overbuild natural gas capacity to rush online, locking in carbon-intensive infrastructure for decades and wasting capital on stranded assets once renewables scale. A third risk: permitting bottlenecks remain unsolved. FERC rules help, but state and local permitting in data center hubs (Virginia, Texas, Arizona) is still a multi-year slog. The queue will get worse before it gets better.
one_sentence: AI made electricity and land scarce again, and the power-and-buildout chain is the trade of the decade.
